id: from One Big Self: "My Dear Conflicted Reader"

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Dear, Conflicted, Reader

outputs.L1:
My Dear Conflicted Reader,

If you will grant me that most of us possess an equivocal nature—and that, upon waking, we have not yet made up our minds which direction we are headed—then you might see a man driving to work in a perfume- and dye-free shirt, and a woman with an overdone tan holding up an orange flag in one hand and a Virginia Slim in the other, as if this were their predestination.

Grant me, too, that both of them were likely contemplating a different scheme of things.

“WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY,” the church marquee demands on the way to my boy’s school, “SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING.”

I admit I had not thought of where, or which direction, in exactly those terms. The radio ministry says g-o-d has a wrong-answer button, and we are all waiting for it to go off...

Count your grey hairs.  
Count your chigger bites.  
Count your pills.  
Count the times the phone rings.  
Count your T cells.  
Count your mosquito bites.  
Count the days since your last menses.  
Count the chickens you’ve eaten.  
Count your cankers.  
Count the storm candles.  
Count your stitches.  
Count your broken bones.  
Count the flies you killed before noon.
outputs.L2:
Dear Troubled Reader,

Suppose you accept that nearly all of us are divided within ourselves, and that on waking we often have no clear decision about the course we mean to take. You might, for instance, notice a man commuting to his job in a shirt free of perfumes and dyes, or a woman with an excessive tan standing with an orange flag in one hand and a Virginia Slim cigarette in the other, as though such roles had been assigned to them by fate. Yet assume, too, that each of them was probably imagining some other possible arrangement of life.

On the route to my son’s school, a church sign asks: WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY, SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING. I confess that I had never considered the matter of destination, or direction, in quite that way. A preacher on the radio says that G-o-d has a button for wrong answers, and that all of us are simply waiting for it to sound.

Tally your gray hairs.  
Tally your chigger bites.  
Tally your pills.  
Tally how many times the telephone rings.  
Tally your T cells.  
Tally your mosquito bites.  
Tally the days since your last period.  
Tally the chickens you have consumed.  
Tally your mouth sores.  
Tally the candles kept for storms.  
Tally your sutures.  
Tally your fractured bones.  
Tally the flies you swatted before midday.
outputs.L3:
The narrator reflects on the conflicted and equivocal nature of human beings, suggesting that people are rarely as simple or consistent as they appear. Ordinary individuals may seem outwardly committed to particular identities, habits, or ways of life, yet inwardly they may imagine alternatives. A person who appears settled in one role may secretly long for another; someone who seems confident in a chosen lifestyle may still be haunted by doubt, desire, or regret. This creates a sense of human life as divided between public appearance and private uncertainty.

Into this ordinary world, religious messages about eternity, judgment, salvation, and damnation intrude unexpectedly. These ideas interrupt the narrator’s daily routine and force larger spiritual questions into the space of everyday life. However, the narrator does not accept these categories easily. Instead, they question the way moral and existential choices are often simplified into rigid oppositions: saved or damned, righteous or sinful, “smoking” or “non-smoking.” By placing a trivial modern distinction beside eternal religious consequences, the narrator exposes the absurdity of reducing complex human experience to neat alternatives.

The repeated commands to “count” intensify this atmosphere of unease. Counting suggests an anxious need to measure, control, and keep track of life, as if existence itself can be managed through numbers. It also evokes mortality: breaths, heartbeats, days, sins, habits, or bodily signs may all be counted down. In this way, the act of counting becomes obsessive, linking the body, routine, and the fear of death. The narrator’s attention to counting reveals a mind preoccupied with both the smallest details of daily life and the largest questions of judgment, meaning, and human uncertainty.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a speaker addressing “you” in a fragmented, unsettled manner, creating the feeling of a mind moving through fear, doubt, and observation all at once. Its second-person voice makes the experience feel both intimate and accusatory, as if the reader is being drawn into a private crisis of conscience. Ordinary details from daily life are placed beside darker reflections on death, judgment, and spiritual consequence, so that the familiar world begins to feel charged with hidden meaning.

A central concern of the text is human uncertainty. The speaker seems unable to rest in a stable interpretation of events. Small signs, gestures, numbers, and repeated actions become objects of attention because they might reveal something larger about fate or divine order. This uncertainty produces moral anxiety: the fear that one’s choices matter in ways that cannot be fully understood, and that a final judgment may be waiting beyond ordinary life. Religious warnings intensify this anxiety by suggesting that human existence is not merely accidental or private, but subject to a greater moral reckoning.

The repeated acts of counting are especially important. Counting appears to be a way of imposing order on confusion, a ritual meant to create certainty in a world that feels unstable. Yet the more the speaker counts, the more obsessive and fragile that control seems. Instead of resolving fear, the counting exposes it. The act becomes a sign of the human desire to measure, classify, and master experience, even when the deepest questions—about death, guilt, salvation, and meaning—remain beyond calculation.

By juxtaposing everyday observations with religious and existential concerns, the text shows how ordinary life can become a site of profound unease. A simple detail may suddenly suggest mortality; a casual action may seem morally significant; a number may appear to carry the weight of destiny. In this way, the text portrays human beings as caught between the desire for certainty and the impossibility of truly possessing it. People search for patterns because they fear randomness, and they seek moral clarity because they fear judgment.

Ultimately, the text suggests that the struggle to find meaning is inseparable from the awareness of death. Mortality makes every action feel potentially significant, while uncertainty prevents any final reassurance. The fragmented style mirrors this condition: thought does not move smoothly, because anxiety interrupts it. The result is a portrait of human life as restless, vulnerable, and morally charged, shaped by the need to understand how one should live in a world where fate, judgment, and meaning remain uncertain.
outputs.L5:
Dear Conflicted Reader,

It is not easy to stand between two choices and feel the weight of both. Sometimes the heart pulls in one direction while the mind quietly argues for another. You may feel uncertain, restless, or even guilty for not knowing what to do. But being conflicted does not mean you are weak—it means you care enough to think deeply.

Give yourself permission to pause. Not every answer arrives quickly, and not every decision is clear at first glance. Listen to your fears, but do not let them lead alone. Listen to your hopes, but ask whether they are rooted in truth. Somewhere between doubt and desire, you may find the quiet voice of your own wisdom.

Dear reader, remember this: confusion is often part of growth. The path ahead may not be perfect, but with honesty, patience, and courage, you can choose a direction and keep moving forward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical essay in the voice of an advice columnist addressed to “My Dear Conflicted Reader,” blending suburban morning observations, religious signage, cigarette imagery, and an obsessive litany beginning with “Count your…”
counterfactuals.output:
My Dear Conflicted Reader,

At 7:12 this morning, the suburbs performed their usual little miracle of denial. Sprinklers ticked like nervous clocks over lawns already green enough to be forgiven. A minivan backed down a driveway with the careful solemnity of a barge leaving harbor. Somewhere, behind a beige curtain, a dog was announcing the mailman before the mailman existed.

You ask me whether to stay or go.

This is the kind of question that arrives in my inbox wearing no shoes. It has crossed wet grass. It has stood under porch lights. It has slept badly. It smells faintly of coffee grounds, laundry detergent, and the cigarette you said you quit but still keep in the glove compartment for weather emergencies, grief emergencies, selfhood emergencies.

My Dear Conflicted Reader, I wish I could tell you there is a clean answer, folded and waiting. I wish I could slide it toward you like a church bulletin.

But even the churches out here have become cryptic.

On Maple Avenue, the Methodist sign reads: GOD HAS A PLAN, but the P is missing, so for three days now it has said GOD HAS A LAN, and I keep imagining heaven as a neighborhood network, all of us poorly connected, buffering under fluorescent clouds.

At the Baptist church near the strip mall: TOO BLESSED TO BE STRESSED.

At the Lutheran church with the red doors: FEAR NOT.

At the gas station: TWO PACKS FOR THE PRICE OF ONE.

Who among us has not mistaken advertising for scripture? Who among us has not stood before a glowing sign and felt, briefly, instructed?

Here is my advice, which may not be advice. Do not trust the answer that makes you feel instantly pure. Purity is often just panic with better posture. Do not trust the answer that requires you to become someone you would not recognize in a grocery store aisle. Do not trust the answer that tastes only of ash.

Still, there is ash.

There is always ash.

There is the ash at the end of the cigarette your neighbor smokes in his bathrobe beside the recycling bins, his face lifted toward the pearled morning as if receiving communion from a small orange coal. There is the ash of things said at midnight, when the kitchen light made everyone look guilty. There is the ash of vows, of birthdays forgotten, of tenderness mishandled, of the version of yourself that once believed love would be enough if only you were good at it.

And there is smoke, too—the shape of what leaves and lingers.

You say you are torn between duty and desire. Let me gently correct you: you are torn between two duties. The duty to keep your promises, and the duty not to disappear inside them. The duty to care for another, and the duty to remain someone capable of care. Desire is not the villain here. Desire is the candle you keep blaming for the darkness.

This morning, the crossing guard stood at the corner in her reflective vest, holding up one gloved hand to stop three lanes of traffic for a boy with a backpack shaped like a dinosaur. Such faith we place in small gestures. A palm raised. A whistle. A painted line. A woman in neon saying: Not yet. Now. Go.

Perhaps that is all discernment is: learning which hand is being raised inside you.

Not yet.

Now.

Go.

Count your exits. Count your excuses. Count your clean towels folded in the hall closet. Count your mother’s warnings and your father’s silences. Count your pills, your passwords, your private tabs, your almosts. Count your blessings if you must, but count also the cost of calling everything a blessing. Count the cigarette butts in the coffee can on the porch. Count the times you said fine and meant frightened. Count the knives in the drawer and the ways you have mistaken sharpness for clarity. Count the rings in the water glass left on the nightstand. Count the prayers you performed without believing and the sins you enjoyed without committing. Count the doors. Count the locks. Count the windows painted shut. Count the mornings you woke and felt your own life beside you like a stranger breathing. Count the tiny mercies: toast, warm socks, the first weak sun on the windshield. Count the lies that protected you until they didn’t. Count the years not as evidence, but as weather. Count your heartbeats when the room goes quiet. Count your ribs. Count your reasons. Count your one wild and unrepeatable name.

And after all that counting, stop.

Numbers can become another form of hiding.

There is a point at which the ledger must be closed and the body consulted. The body, that old suburban prophet, mowing the same patch of fear every Saturday. The body knows which house feels like shelter and which like storage. The body knows the difference between peace and anesthesia. The body knows when a kiss has become a receipt.

You do not need to set fire to your life to see by it. You do not need to stay cold to prove you are loyal. You do not need to confuse suffering with depth. Even Christ, if we are allowed to mention him beneath the buzzing power lines and the patriotic banners at the car wash, asked whether the cup might pass from him.

Asking was not failure.

My Dear Conflicted Reader, begin smaller than the decision. Begin with one honest sentence spoken aloud in an empty car. Begin with the cigarette unlit between your fingers. Begin with the church sign missing its letter. Begin with the possibility that guidance may arrive misspelled, half-burned, smelling of rain and gasoline.

Say: I am afraid.

Say: I want.

Say: I have stayed.

Say: I may leave.

Say: I am still worthy of morning.

Then watch what happens in you. Not in the room. Not on their face. In you.

The sprinklers will finish their silver gossip. The school bus will sigh open its doors. The man in the bathrobe will crush his cigarette beneath one slipper and go back inside to whatever waits for him there. The signs will keep changing. God will remain badly advertised and everywhere.

And you, dear one, will have to live.

That is the harshest counsel and the holiest: not stay, not go, but live—so fully that whichever door you choose will know it was opened by someone awake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a fragmented prose-poem about mortality, faith, health anxiety, and daily errands, including a church marquee that says “WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY / SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING” and ending with a list of things to count.
counterfactuals.output:
At the red light, my heart misfires once and I become a cathedral of alarms.

The pharmacy sign blinks: FLU SHOTS. PASSPORT PHOTOS. BLOOD PRESSURE.  
As if the body were a country I might still be allowed to enter with the right documents.

I buy toothpaste, bananas, a roll of stamps I will never use, antacids shaped like little moons. The cashier asks if I found everything okay. I say yes, though I am missing several certainties and possibly a thyroid.

Outside, the day is almost beautiful. This is one of its cruelties.

A crow walks through the parking lot with priestly confidence. Somewhere, someone is being told it’s benign. Somewhere else, the opposite. I press two fingers to my wrist and wait for the tiny drum to prove I am still invited.

On the corner, the church marquee says:

WHERE DO YOU WANT TO SPEND ETERNITY  
SMOKING OR NON-SMOKING

I laugh, then feel guilty for laughing, then wonder if guilt is just faith with its coat on inside out.

My grandmother believed the dead watched over us. My mother believes in taking vitamin D. I believe in checking the mole again under better light.

At home, the mail is mostly offers: better insurance, cheaper windows, salvation by refinancing. The dog needs walking. The sink needs scrubbing. The soul, if present, is being asked to hold while I compare unit prices.

Lord, if you are there, forgive me for making an idol of my pulse. Forgive me for every ambulance I have followed with my imagination. Forgive me for wanting a sign and then distrusting signage.

The body says: notice me.  
The spirit says: notice me.  
The dishwasher says: unload me.

Evening lowers itself gently over the neighborhood, as if not to startle the dying, which is all of us, which is a fact I can only touch briefly before needing to fold towels.

I take my pills with tap water. I bless the water by needing it.

Before sleep, I make bargains no theology would endorse: one more year for kindness, one clear scan for belief, one ordinary Tuesday in exchange for all my grand opinions about suffering.

The ceiling keeps its counsel.

In the dark, I count:

breaths,  
sirens,  
refills remaining,  
unanswered prayers,  
ceiling cracks,  
vitamins in the palm,  
days since the last appointment,  
sparrows on the wire,  
the living,  
the dead,  
the small errands still to do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of a contemporary American literary nonfiction piece: intimate, wry, slightly surreal, with hyphenated line breaks, a parent driving a child to school, radio evangelism, and a final catalog of bodily and domestic reckonings.
counterfactuals.output:
The road to school was lined with winter trees doing their best impression of moral instruction—bare, uplifted, accusatory. My daughter sat in the back seat with one sock higher than the other, eating dry cereal from a plastic cup and explaining that Tuesday was the worst day because it had “no costume.”

“What about Wednesday?” I asked.

“Wednesday has hope,” she said, and looked out the window as if hope were a strip mall we might be passing.

On the radio, a man with a voice like a polished walnut was telling us the end was near, though near, in his case, had sponsors. He said the family was under attack. He said the body was a temple. He said a donation of any amount would help keep the message alive. Between sentences, there was the soft electric hush of invisible money.

My daughter asked if temples had bathrooms.

“Yes,” I said. “Probably.”

“Then your body can’t be a temple,” she said. “Because you always say you need five minutes and then you take your phone.”

There are mornings when parenting feels less like stewardship than like being cross-examined by a small, beloved prosecutor wearing glitter sneakers. The light turned red. A man in the next lane was shaving with an electric razor, his face tilted toward his rearview mirror in the grave and private ritual of becoming acceptable. Behind him, a dog stood with both paws on the window, staring at me as if it remembered me from another life and was disappointed.

The preacher said: Are you ready?

My daughter said: For what?

The light changed. We went on.

At the drop-off lane, the school had arranged itself into the usual civic ballet: minivans sighing, children spilling out with backpacks too large for their bodies, teachers waving like air-traffic controllers of the soul. I kissed the top of my daughter’s head and got a mouthful of static hair.

“Be kind,” I said, because it is the parent’s standard morning benediction, meaning: survive and do not become evidence against me.

“Be normal,” she said, and climbed out.

Then she turned back, one hand on the car door.

“Actually,” she said, “don’t.”

The door slammed with the blunt certainty of childhood. She joined the river of children moving toward the building, each of them carrying some impossible weather inside. I watched until she disappeared through the doors, though disappearance is not the right word. Children do not disappear. They are absorbed. By school, by language, by other people’s songs.

On the radio, the preacher had moved on to forgiveness. He sounded exhausted by it. Forgiveness, he said, is not a feeling but a choice. I considered this while a crossing guard in a neon vest held up one white-gloved hand against traffic, stopping us all with the tired authority of an angel assigned to municipal work.

I drove home under a sky the color of dishwater, past the pharmacy, the church with the digital sign—GOD ANSWERS KNEE-MAIL—and the donut shop where men in work boots stood in line for sugared rings of consolation. The preacher faded into static, then surged back, saying blood, saying mercy, saying call now.

At home, the house waited in its theatrical silence: breakfast bowls lacquered with milk, a sweater inside out on the couch, the dishwasher blinking its little red accusation. I stood in the kitchen with my coat still on. The dog, who had eaten something unholy in the yard, looked at me with the damp sincerity of a penitent.

There was, as always, a reckoning.

The coffee gone cold in the mug; the orange rind curled like a small dead animal on the counter; the permission slip unsigned beneath a magnet from Niagara Falls; the bruise on my thigh of unknown origin; the ache in my jaw from clenching through dreams; the laundry, damp and faintly sour, waiting to be moved from one machine to another as if migration itself were redemption; the hair in the drain; the cracked heel; the pill bottle with three left; the lunchbox fermenting in a backpack; the bedsheet twisted into a rope; the dust on the baseboards; the soft stomach under the shirt; the unpaid bill; the onion sprouting green in the dark cabinet; the child’s cereal dust in the back seat; the gospel of crumbs; the temple with its bathroom, its locked closets, its flickering lights; the body asking, again, to be forgiven for being a body; the house asking, again, to be entered and endured.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental monologue to a “Conflicted Reader” about equivocation, predestination, smoking, illness, and apocalypse, using long winding sentences followed by a chant-like inventory of anxieties.
counterfactuals.output:
Conflicted Reader, you who hold the page at a slight remove as though it might cough, you who suspect every sentence of carrying a hidden fever, every doctrine of concealing a trapdoor, every kindness of being merely another technique of persuasion, listen: equivocation is not only the coward’s weather but also the climate of the condemned, the fog in which a person who has been told that all roads were paved before his birth still keeps turning left and right with theatrical seriousness, as if choice were a cigarette he could quit tomorrow, as if tomorrow were not already written in the ash.

You ask whether predestination absolves the hand that strikes the match, whether the match absolves the lung, whether the lung absolves the hunger that drew the smoke down into its pink, branching chapel, and I tell you I do not know, which is either honesty or evasion, and this is the whole trouble: that every “perhaps” has a collar, every “however” a small black hood, every “on the other hand” another hand behind it, pushing us steadily toward the door marked END while we continue to debate the typography.

I have watched men smoke outside hospitals, not defiantly, not even sadly, but with the mild administrative patience of clerks waiting for an office to reopen, their gowns flapping at the knee, their IV poles beside them like thin metallic saints, and I have thought that the body is an apocalyptic text written in abbreviations: CT, MRI, BP, WBC, and the reader, poor reader, conflicted reader, must decide whether the diagnosis is a prophecy, a punishment, a clerical error, or simply another weather report from the kingdom of flesh.

Do not imagine I am accusing you, though accusation hangs in the room like stale smoke; do not imagine I am comforting you, though comfort keeps pawing at the door; I am merely standing here in the flicker between catastrophe and explanation, saying that illness makes theologians of us all, not because we suddenly believe in God, but because we begin to believe in causes, in secret courts, in verdicts pronounced before the symptoms, in a book where our coughing was annotated before we learned to breathe.

And if the apocalypse comes, it will not come as advertised, not with horsemen punctual against the horizon, not with trumpets splitting the municipal sky, but as a series of equivocations: a rash that is probably nothing, a heat wave that is merely seasonal, a plume that is not technically toxic, a war that has not officially begun, a cough that is just a cough until it is a bell, and then the bell will say what bells have always said, which is not “repent” exactly, nor “flee,” exactly, but “now, now, now,” that most unbearable doctrine.

So smoke if you must, Conflicted Reader, or do not smoke; be chosen, or choose; call the sickness fate, call it negligence, call it inheritance, call it metaphor, call it the body’s weather finally turning literal; only know that the mouth is an altar that can bless or burn, and the future, whether fixed or fluid, keeps arriving with the patience of a nurse who has already seen your chart.

And now let us count what trembles.

The fear of the lung.  
The fear of the page.  
The fear of the sealed envelope.  
The fear of the open verdict.  
The fear of the cough in the next room.  
The fear of smoke under the door.  
The fear of desire disguised as habit.  
The fear of habit disguised as destiny.  
The fear of destiny disguised as choice.  
The fear of choice arriving too late.  
The fear of the doctor’s pause.  
The fear of the scan’s pale moon.  
The fear of cells in secret congress.  
The fear of mercy with conditions.  
The fear of judgment without language.  
The fear of “benign.”  
The fear of “progressive.”  
The fear of “incurable.”  
The fear of “we’ll know more soon.”  
The fear of a sky too orange at noon.  
The fear of birds going quiet.  
The fear of clocks continuing.  
The fear of clocks stopping.  
The fear of being spared.  
The fear of not being spared.  
The fear of the last cigarette.  
The fear of wanting another.  
The fear of having been written.  
The fear of having written oneself.  
The fear of the trumpet.  
The fear of no trumpet.  
The fear of smoke.  
The fear of breath.  
The fear of breath.  
The fear of breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem that starts “My Dear Conflicted Reader,” asks the reader to grant that people have equivocal natures, includes vivid mundane details like a dye-free shirt, an orange flag, Virginia Slims, and closes with repeated “Count your” lines.
counterfactuals.output:
My Dear Conflicted Reader, grant me this: that people have equivocal natures, that the hand which steadies the ladder may also shake the jar of moths, that tenderness and ruin can share a kitchen chair beneath the same buzzing light. I have seen a woman in a dye-free shirt rinse blueberries in a chipped white bowl as if absolution were a domestic task. I have seen an orange flag snap at the edge of a construction site, bright as warning, bright as permission, while a man smoked Virginia Slims beside a stack of cinder blocks and called his mother from a phone with a cracked screen. The afternoon went on being ordinary. Cars coughed at the curb. A dog worried a paper cup. Somewhere, a child practiced the recorder badly enough to make the air more human. What are we to do with our double hearts, our clean laundry and our secret knives, our apologies folded into drawers with the socks? Even the saint pockets a little envy. Even the thief waters the fern. So do not ask for a verdict too early. Let the rain finish darkening the sidewalk. Let the kettle click off. Let the cigarette burn down in its narrow cathedral of ash.

Count your bruises.

Count your blessings.

Count your exits.

Count your hands, still empty, still yours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
